title: The Roman Republic
description: An illustrated map of the Roman Republic, from the traditional founding of Rome and the expulsion of the kings through the conquest of Italy, the three wars with Carthage, Hannibal at Cannae and the fall of Carthage to the Gracchi, Sulla, Caesar in Gaul, the Ides of March and the rise of Augustus.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Roman Republic, 509 to 27 BCE
note: Based mainly on Livy, Polybius, Plutarch, Caesar’s own Commentaries, Suetonius and Appian, on inscriptions and on archaeology; each chapter says which it follows. The traditional dates for Rome’s first centuries were written down long afterwards. Ancient figures for armies and deaths are often too large and are given as theirs. Native names are Latin. The map is stylised and not to scale; coasts are drawn as they are today, and some ancient harbours have silted up. The Powers layer is painted loosely.

steps.title: Rome, city of kings
steps.text: Tradition says Romulus founded Rome in 753 BCE on hills beside the Tiber, and that seven kings followed. The last, Tarquin the Proud, was driven out in 509 BCE, and Rome became a republic (res publica, “public thing”). Roman writers set down these dates centuries later; archaeology shows a growing town by the 6th century BCE.
steps.today: Today: Rome, Italy; the Forum and Palatine Hill are an archaeological park.

steps.title: Consuls, Senate and the Twelve Tables
steps.text: Two consuls, elected each year, replaced the king, advised by the Senate. Poorer citizens (plebeians) struggled against the old families (patricians) and, by tradition, walked out of the city in 494 BCE until they won their own officers, the tribunes. Rome’s first written laws, the Twelve Tables, date from about 450 BCE.
steps.today: Today: Rome; fragments of the Twelve Tables survive only as quotations in later writers.

steps.title: Conquering Italy
steps.text: Rome fought the Samnites of the central Apennines in three wars. In 321 BCE a Roman army was trapped in a narrow pass, the Caudine Forks, and forced to surrender and walk under a yoke of spears. Rome still won, laid roads such as the Appian Way and planted colonies. By 264 BCE it led nearly all Italy.
steps.today: Today: near Arpaia and Montesarchio, Campania; the exact pass is disputed.

steps.title: Pyrrhus and the Greek south
steps.text: Tarentum, a Greek city in the south, asked King Pyrrhus of Epirus for help against Rome. His army, with war elephants, won at Heraclea and Asculum but lost so many men that a costly victory is still called “Pyrrhic”. He left Italy after Beneventum in 275 BCE, and Tarentum fell to Rome in 272 BCE.

steps.title: A fleet to beat Carthage
steps.text: Rome and Carthage, the great sea power of the west, fought over Sicily from 264 BCE. Rome built its first big fleet, and Polybius says boarding bridges won it the battle of Mylae in 260. At the Aegates Islands in 241 BCE a new fleet sank Carthage’s supply convoy. Carthage paid an indemnity and left Sicily.
steps.today: Today: off Trapani, western Sicily, Italy; the islands include Favignana.

steps.title: Hannibal crosses the Alps
steps.text: In 218 BCE Hannibal Barca led an army from Spain over the Alps, with elephants, to strike Rome at home. Polybius says about 46,000 men set out and about 26,000 reached Italy; his figures are disputed. Which pass he used is also disputed, and the Col de la Traversette is one candidate. Most elephants did not survive.
steps.today: Today: the French and Italian Alps; no pass is proven.

steps.title: Cannae
steps.text: On the plain of Cannae in Apulia, Hannibal’s smaller army enveloped a Roman army of about 80,000, by Polybius’s count. Polybius gives some 70,000 Roman dead; other counts are lower, and all are disputed. It was Rome’s worst defeat. Yet Rome refused terms, raised new legions and slowly wore Hannibal down in Italy.
steps.today: Today: near Barletta, Puglia, Italy; an archaeological site.

steps.title: Scipio defeats Hannibal
steps.text: Publius Cornelius Scipio, later called Africanus, took the war to Africa in 204 BCE. At Zama in 202 BCE he beat Hannibal, helped by Numidian cavalry under his ally Masinissa. Carthage gave up its fleet and overseas lands and paid tribute for fifty years. The exact site of the battle is uncertain. Rome now ruled the western Mediterranean.
steps.today: Today: in Tunisia; scholars place Zama at several sites.

steps.title: Carthage must be destroyed
steps.text: Cato the Elder is said to have ended his speeches with “Carthage must be destroyed”. After a siege of about two years, Scipio Aemilianus broke in during 146 BCE. Most survivors were enslaved, and the land became the province of Africa. The same year Rome sacked Corinth. The story that Romans sowed Carthage with salt is not in ancient sources.
steps.today: Today: Carthage, a suburb of Tunis, Tunisia; a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Gracchi, Marius and Sulla
steps.text: Tiberius Gracchus, a tribune, proposed land for poor citizens and was beaten to death by senators in 133 BCE; his brother Gaius died in 121. Gaius Marius then let landless men join the legions, who looked to their general for pay and land. In 88 BCE Sulla marched on Rome, the first general to do so.
steps.today: Today: Rome; the Forum, where the Gracchi died, can be visited.

steps.title: Caesar in Gaul
steps.text: Julius Caesar conquered Gaul in eight years of war, which he told in his Commentaries. In 52 BCE he besieged the Gallic leader Vercingetorix at Alesia, building siege lines against the town and a vast relief army. Vercingetorix surrendered and was executed years later. Caesar’s fame and loyal legions now made him a danger to the Senate.
steps.today: Today: Alise-Sainte-Reine, Burgundy, France; the site has a museum.

steps.title: Crossing the Rubicon
steps.text: In January 49 BCE the Senate ordered Caesar to give up his army. He led one legion over the Rubicon, the boundary of his province, and civil war began. Pompey fled to Greece, where Caesar beat him at Pharsalus in 48 BCE; Pompey was then killed in Egypt. The Rubicon’s exact course is uncertain.
steps.today: Today: near Rimini, Emilia-Romagna, Italy; several streams claim the name.

steps.title: The Ides of March
steps.text: Caesar was made dictator for life early in 44 BCE. On the Ides of March, Suetonius says more than sixty senators, led by Brutus and Cassius, were in the plot, and they stabbed him in a hall beside Pompey’s theatre. They hoped to save the Republic. They only started new civil wars.
steps.today: Today: Largo di Torre Argentina, Rome, where the ruins of Pompey’s Curia lie.

steps.title: Actium and Augustus
steps.text: In 31 BCE Octavian, Caesar’s adopted heir, beat Mark Antony and Cleopatra in the naval battle of Actium; both died in Egypt in 30 BCE. In 27 BCE the Senate gave him the name Augustus. He kept the old offices and the Senate but held the real power, and the Republic gave way to the Empire.

items.role: The state of Rome: a republic (res publica) run by elected magistrates and the Senate, which grew from one city to ruler of the Mediterranean.

ties.text: Leads the Latin and Italian allies (socii)

items.name: Hannibal Barca
items.text: Hannibal, son of the general Hamilcar Barca, took command of Carthage’s army in Spain at about 26. He led it over the Alps, beat Rome at Trasimene and Cannae, and stayed in Italy for fifteen years. Defeated at Zama, he later fled east and, Roman writers say, took poison to avoid capture.

items.name: Scipio Africanus
items.text: Scipio survived Cannae as a young officer, then took Spain from Carthage and carried the war to Africa. His victory at Zama in 202 BCE earned him the name Africanus. Later accused of taking bribes, he left Rome for a country villa, where he is said to have died. His adopted grandson later destroyed Carthage.

items.name: Cato the Elder
items.text: Cato was a self-made senator, known as a stern guardian of old Roman habits. His treatise on farming is the oldest surviving Latin prose book. He served as censor in 184 BCE. Plutarch says he ended speeches with “Carthage must be destroyed”. He died in 149 BCE, the year the Third Punic War began.

items.name: Tiberius Gracchus
items.text: Tiberius, grandson of Scipio Africanus through his mother, was elected tribune in 133 BCE. He proposed to share out public land held by the rich among poor citizens. When he stood for a second term, senators and their followers clubbed him to death. Many historians date the Republic’s long crisis from his killing.

items.name: Julius Caesar
items.text: Caesar rose through politics and debt to command in Gaul. His Commentaries, written in plain Latin, remain a model of prose. After defeating Pompey he reformed the calendar, a version of which we still use, and was made dictator for life. Conspirators killed him weeks later, on 15 March 44 BCE.

items.name: Augustus
items.native: Gaius Octavius, later Imperator Caesar Augustus
items.text: Born Gaius Octavius, he was Caesar’s great-nephew and adopted heir. At 19 he raised an army, joined Antony to hunt Caesar’s killers, then beat Antony at Actium. As Augustus he ruled for over forty years, keeping the forms of the Republic. He died at Nola in 14 CE, and Rome honoured him as a god.
